plan: First digital-SAT Reading and Writing batch: 10 short texts, one question each. Craft and Structure 3 (word in context, function, cross-text), Information and Ideas 3 (central idea, quantitative evidence, inference), Standard English Conventions 2 (boundaries, agreement), Expression of Ideas 2 (transition, rhetorical synthesis). People and places are invented, and the factual premises are well established.

passages.title: Greenhouse (original fiction)
passages.text:
The following text is from an original short story.
Marisol had expected the abandoned greenhouse to be empty, but it was ______ with life: ferns crowded every bench, and vines had climbed all the way to the cracked glass roof.

passages.title: Foundations
passages.text: Bridges are usually admired for their spans, the distances between their supports. Engineer Tomás Reyes, however, argues that the most important part of a bridge is the part no one sees: its foundation. "A long span on a weak foundation," he says, "is simply a dramatic way to fail."

passages.title: Learning words (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Some teachers argue that the fastest way for students to build vocabulary is to memorize lists of words and their definitions. Students can review dozens of words in a single sitting, and quiz scores often rise within days.

Text 2
Researchers who study reading point out that definitions memorized for a quiz are often forgotten within weeks. Words met repeatedly in meaningful reading, by contrast, tend to be retained, because readers see how the words are actually used.

passages.title: Repair café
passages.text: Once a month, a community center in the town of Alder Creek hosts a "repair café," where volunteers fix residents' broken lamps, toasters, and bicycles for free. Organizers say the event keeps hundreds of items out of the landfill each year. Just as important, they add, residents who watch the repairs often learn to fix similar problems on their own.

passages.title: Feeder survey
passages.text:
A student counted the birds visiting three feeders in her yard over four weeks. Each feeder held a different food.
Feeder | Food | Total visits
1 | Sunflower seeds | 212
2 | Thistle seeds | 87
3 | Suet | 145
The student concluded that, of the three foods, sunflower seeds attracted the most visits.

passages.title: Shell chains
passages.text: Marine biologists have observed that when an empty shell larger than any in a group appears, hermit crabs nearby often line up by size beside it. When the largest crab moves into the new shell, the next crab in line takes the shell it left behind, and so on down the line. This pattern suggests that ______

passages.title: Canal town
passages.text: The town's first canal opened in ______ within ten years, the number of businesses along its route had tripled.

passages.title: Letters
passages.text: The collection of letters, which spans four decades and includes notes from dozens of correspondents, ______ historians a rare view of daily life in the port city.

passages.title: Coquí frogs
passages.text: Most frogs lay their eggs in water, where the young hatch as swimming tadpoles. The coquí frogs of Puerto Rico, ______ lay their eggs on land, and the young hatch as tiny, fully formed frogs.

passages.title: Recycling notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Glass bottles and plastic bottles can both be recycled.
• Glass can be recycled again and again without losing quality.
• Most plastics can be recycled only a few times before the material degrades.
• Recycled glass is often used to make new bottles.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: ferns crowded every bench, and vines had climbed all the way to the cracked glass roof
candidates.explanation: The colon introduces evidence that the greenhouse was full of plants. "Teeming with life" means crowded with living things, which matches ferns on every bench and vines up to the roof.

B.rationale: "Devoid" means completely lacking, the opposite of what the details describe.

C.rationale: "Reminiscent" means suggestive of something else and is followed by "of," not "with"; it does not describe abundance.

D.rationale: "Wary" means cautious, a quality of people or animals, not of a greenhouse.

hints: What do the details after the colon show about the greenhouse?
Predict a word meaning 'full of' before reading the choices.

strategy.explanation: Predict "full," then choose the closest precise word.

candidates.remember: Let the text's evidence choose the word.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the quotation in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It presents a counterargument that Reyes goes on to reject.
choices.B: It explains how engineers measure the span of a bridge.
choices.C: It illustrates, in memorable terms, why Reyes believes a bridge's foundation matters more than its span.
choices.D: It suggests that most existing bridges were built on weak foundations.

candidates.evidence: "A long span on a weak foundation," he says, "is simply a dramatic way to fail."
candidates.explanation: Reyes claims the foundation is the most important part of a bridge. The quotation backs that claim with a vivid image: however impressive the span, a weak foundation means failure.

A.rationale: The quotation is Reyes's own statement supporting his view, not a counterargument.

B.rationale: The quotation says nothing about how spans are measured.

D.rationale: The quotation describes a hypothetical case and makes no claim about most existing bridges.

hints: What is Reyes's main claim?
How does the quotation relate to that claim?

strategy.explanation: Identify the claim first, then ask how the quotation serves it.

candidates.remember: Function questions ask what a part does for the whole.

author_checklist.note: Reyes is an invented engineer; the claim is presented as his opinion

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?

choices.A: They would argue that quizzes are the most reliable way to measure vocabulary growth.
choices.B: They would grant that memorizing lists can raise quiz scores quickly but question whether those gains last.
choices.C: They would claim that students cannot learn any new words by memorizing lists.
choices.D: They would suggest that reading builds vocabulary faster than memorizing lists does.

candidates.evidence: definitions memorized for a quiz are often forgotten within weeks
candidates.explanation: Text 1 claims lists are the fastest way to build vocabulary, citing quick quiz gains. Text 2 does not deny quick gains; it says memorized definitions are often forgotten within weeks, while words met in reading tend to stick. So the researchers would accept the short-term gains but doubt they last.

A.rationale: Text 2 implies quiz results can mislead, since memorized words fade; it does not call quizzes the most reliable measure.

C.rationale: Text 2 says memorized words are "often forgotten," not that students learn none; "cannot learn any" goes too far.

D.rationale: Text 2 argues that reading leads to better retention, not faster learning.

hints: Does Text 2 deny that lists raise quiz scores?
What does Text 2 say happens weeks later?

strategy.explanation: Find where Text 2 addresses memorized definitions, then pick the response that matches its partial agreement.

candidates.remember: Watch for partial agreement and extreme wording.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The repair café in Alder Creek mainly repairs bicycles.
choices.B: A monthly event in Alder Creek reduces waste and helps residents learn to fix things themselves.
choices.C: Volunteers in Alder Creek are paid to repair residents' household items.
choices.D: Residents of Alder Creek throw away fewer items than residents of other towns do.

candidates.evidence: Organizers say the event keeps hundreds of items out of the landfill each year. Just as important, they add, residents who watch the repairs often learn to fix similar problems on their own.
candidates.explanation: The text describes the repair café and its two benefits: keeping items out of the landfill and teaching residents repair skills. B captures both.

A.rationale: Bicycles are one example among several; the text does not say they are the main focus.

C.rationale: The repairs are done for free by volunteers; nothing says the volunteers are paid.

D.rationale: The text makes no comparison with other towns.

hints: What is the whole text about?
Which choice includes both benefits the organizers mention?

strategy.explanation: Summarize in one sentence, then match.

candidates.remember: The main idea covers the whole text, not one example.

author_checklist.dup_note: chosen over a library-lending topic, which resembled an app fixture passage

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's conclusion?

choices.A: Feeder 1, which held sunflower seeds, had 212 visits, more than either the thistle feeder (87) or the suet feeder (145).
choices.B: Feeder 2, which held thistle seeds, had 87 visits, fewer than Feeder 3.
choices.C: Together, the three feeders received 444 visits.
choices.D: Feeder 3, which held suet, had 145 visits.

candidates.explanation: The conclusion is that sunflower seeds attracted the most visits. Supporting it requires comparing the sunflower feeder with both others: 212 is greater than 87 and 145. Only A makes that full comparison.

B.rationale: This compares only the other two feeders and says nothing about sunflower seeds.

C.rationale: The total does not show which food attracted the most visits.

D.rationale: One feeder's count alone cannot show which food was most popular.

hints: What exactly does the conclusion claim?
Which choice compares sunflower seeds with both other foods?

strategy.explanation: Restate the claim, then choose the data that compares all three.

candidates.remember: A 'most' claim needs a comparison with every other option.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: hermit crabs generally prefer shells that are too small for them.
choices.B: only the largest crab in the group ends up with a better-fitting shell.
choices.C: hermit crabs line up beside a new shell without regard to their size.
choices.D: a single new shell can lead to several crabs in the group moving into larger shells.

candidates.evidence: When the largest crab moves into the new shell, the next crab in line takes the shell it left behind, and so on down the line.
candidates.explanation: Each crab that moves leaves its old shell for the next crab, and the chain continues down the line. So one new shell lets many crabs upgrade, not just one.

A.rationale: The crabs move into larger shells, which suggests they seek a better fit, not smaller shells.

B.rationale: The chain of moves means crabs after the largest one also get larger shells.

C.rationale: The text says the crabs line up by size.

hints: Follow the chain: what happens to each shell that is left behind?
How many crabs end up in a new shell?

strategy.explanation: Trace the sequence in the second sentence to its result.

candidates.remember: Completion questions follow the text's logic to its next step.

author_checklist.fact_note: shell vacancy chains in hermit crabs are a well-documented behavior; no researcher is named

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: within ten years, the number of businesses along its route had tripled.
candidates.explanation: "The town's first canal opened in 1825" and "within ten years, the number of businesses along its route had tripled" are both independent clauses. A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses.

A.rationale: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.

C.rationale: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

D.rationale: "Which" makes the second part a relative clause, but the rest of the sentence ("within ten years, the number … had tripled") cannot follow "which" grammatically.

hints: Is each part of the sentence a complete sentence on its own?
What punctuation can join two complete sentences without a conjunction?

strategy.explanation: Two independent clauses with no conjunction need a semicolon or a period.

candidates.remember: Semicolon: two complete sentences, no conjunction.

author_checklist.note: no colon or period option is offered, so exactly one choice is correct

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The collection of letters, which spans four decades and includes notes from dozens of correspondents,
candidates.explanation: The subject is "collection," which is singular; "of letters" and the clause between commas are modifiers. The singular verb "offers" agrees, and the clause's own verbs ("spans," "includes") confirm the singular subject.

A.rationale: "Offer" is plural, agreeing with "letters" or "correspondents" rather than the subject "collection."

hints: Cross out the phrase and clause that describe the subject.
Is "collection" singular or plural?

strategy.explanation: Strip it down to "The collection … ______ historians a rare view"; only the singular verb fits.

candidates.remember: Find the true subject, then match the verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: Most frogs lay their eggs in water, where the young hatch as swimming tadpoles.
candidates.explanation: The first sentence describes most frogs; the second describes coquí frogs doing the opposite (eggs on land, no tadpoles). "However" signals that contrast.

A.rationale: Coquí frogs are an exception to the pattern, not an example of it.

B.rationale: The coquí's behavior is not a result of what most frogs do.

D.rationale: "Similarly" signals likeness, but the coquí differs from most frogs.

hints: Is the coquí like most frogs or different from them?
Choose the transition that signals that relationship.

strategy.explanation: Predict a contrast word such as 'but,' then match.

candidates.remember: Name the relationship before choosing the transition.

author_checklist.fact_note: coquí frogs (Eleutherodactylus) lay eggs on land and develop directly without a tadpole stage

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between recycling glass and recycling plastic. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Glass bottles and plastic bottles can both be recycled.
choices.B: Recycled glass is often used to make new bottles.
choices.C: Both glass and plastic are commonly used to make bottles, and both can be recycled.
choices.D: Glass can be recycled again and again without losing quality, whereas most plastics can be recycled only a few times before the material degrades.

candidates.evidence: Glass can be recycled again and again without losing quality.
candidates.explanation: The goal is a difference. D contrasts how many times each material can be recycled, using "whereas" to make the difference explicit.

A.rationale: This states a similarity, not a difference.

B.rationale: This gives information about glass only, with no comparison to plastic.

C.rationale: This states similarities between the materials.

hints: The goal is to emphasize a difference.
Which choice mentions both materials and contrasts them?

strategy.explanation: Underline the goal (difference), then eliminate choices that state similarities or mention one material.

candidates.remember: Synthesis questions: the stated goal decides the answer.
